content: In 2020, only one-third of children under five years of age who were eligible for tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment (TPT) actually received it. This highlights a significant gap in case detection and treatment. Additionally, over half a million older adolescents (aged 15–19 years) are estimated to develop TB annually. The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the World Health Organization (WHO) End TB Strategy aim to reduce TB incidence by 80% and TB-related deaths by 90% by 2030, compared to 2015 levels. By 2022, the global commitment included providing TPT to at least 30 million people, including 4 million child contacts under five years of age, 20 million other household contacts (including children over five), and 6 million people living with HIV. To address TB in children and adolescents, WHO published the second edition of its guidance for national TB programs in 2014. Since then, new evidence and recommendations have emerged, leading to updates in TB prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care models. In 2021, WHO convened a Guideline Development Group (GDG) to review this new evidence, including data from a randomized controlled trial on treatment shortening for children with non-severe TB. This resulted in updated recommendations for managing TB in children and adolescents. The 2022 consolidated guidelines incorporate new evidence-based recommendations, including those from other WHO TB guidelines issued since 2014. These updates aim to provide policymakers and healthcare providers with comprehensive guidance on TB prevention, case detection, and treatment for children and adolescents. The guidelines also emphasize reducing TB-related morbidity and mortality in alignment with global targets, such as the SDGs and the End TB Strategy. The target audience for these guidelines includes national TB programs, primary healthcare providers, maternal and child health programs, national AIDS programs, pediatricians, clinicians, and organizations working in TB, HIV, and infectious diseases. The guidelines also address the needs of community-based organizations, technical partners, and policymakers. The 2022 guidelines represent a significant update compared to the 2014 version. They include new recommendations based on Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes (PICO) questions, as well as existing recommendations relevant to children and adolescents. Key updates include guidance on TB screening, diagnostic approaches, treatment regimens, and care models. For example, new recommendations support the use of shorter treatment regimens for non-severe TB, all-oral regimens for drug-resistant TB, and integrated family-centered care models. The guidelines also emphasize the importance of childand adolescent-friendly services to improve access to high-quality care. They consolidate recommendations on TB screening, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, ensuring alignment with the latest evidence and global priorities. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated as new evidence becomes available, with a planned review within five years. The scope of the guidelines focuses on children under 10 years of age and adolescents aged 10–19 years. Evidence-based interventions are recommended at each stage to reduce TB transmission, enable early diagnosis, and optimize treatment outcomes. The guidelines also address specific challenges, such as TB in children with HIV, malnutrition, and TB meningitis. They provide recommendations on diagnostic tools, including the use of Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirates and stool samples, and treatment regimens for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB. Additionally, they highlight the importance of decentralized and family-centered care models to improve TB prevention and treatment coverage. WHO has outlined dissemination strategies for these guidelines, including webinars, training materials, and technical support for countries. Monitoring and evaluation will focus on TB notification rates, treatment outcomes, and TPT coverage among eligible children and adolescents. The guidelines aim to support global efforts to end TB and improve outcomes for children and adolescents affected by the disease.
